chapters.title: Chapter 3: Risk, Returns and the Power Law

lessons.title: Why Most Startups Fail and What That Means for Your Capital

children.text: Dunzo was the first Indian startup Google invested in directly, and it went on to raise more than $450 million, with Reliance among its backers. It still collapsed, leaving employees and vendors unpaid. Koo, the homegrown microblogging app backed by Accel and Tiger Global, was valued at about $285 million in 2022 and shut down in July 2024. If companies with that much money and those investors can fail, the pre-seed startup pitching you on WhatsApp certainly can. This lesson looks at why startups actually die, what an angel gets back when they do, and the portfolio rules that follow.

body.text: Running out of cash is how startups die, not why. The real cause is almost always something an angel could have asked about: no genuine demand, broken unit economics, bad timing or founders who should not have been trusted.

children.text: What the Post-Mortems Say
Research firm CB Insights studied post-mortems from 431 venture-backed companies that shut down from 2023 onwards. Most failures had more than one cause, so the percentages add up to more than 100%.

body.title: Most cited reasons for startup failure (% of shutdowns, CB Insights)

body.text: "Ran out of capital" tops the list, but it is the final symptom, like a death certificate that says "heart stopped". The useful question is why the money ran out and no one would put in more. That is where the other reasons come in, and they are exactly what your diligence should probe before you invest.

children.text: Four Root Causes, Four Indian Stories

markDefs.definition: The point where a product meets a real, lasting need: customers keep using it and are willing to pay without heavy discounts or persuasion.
The revenue and costs attached to a single unit of business, such as one order or one customer. If each unit loses money, growing faster only loses money faster.

children.text: Two terms come up in almost every failure story.
Product-market fit
asks whether people genuinely need the product.
Unit economics
asks whether the company makes or loses money each time it serves them.

body.caption: Root causes of failure and the question that exposes each one
headers: The question an angel should ask

cells: No sustainable business behind the users
Downloads and sign-ups grow, but revenue does not follow and costs keep rising
Koo: large user base and top-tier investors, shut in July 2024 after acquisition talks with Dailyhunt collapsed; its founders cited the high cost of running a social media app
"Do users come back without incentives, and who will pay, how much, and when?"
Broken unit economics
Every order or customer loses money after delivery, discounts and marketing
Dunzo: pivoted from hyperlocal delivery into capital-hungry quick commerce with its own dark stores, and collapsed despite raising more than $450 million
"After all variable costs, does each order make or lose money, and what has to change for it to make money?"
Bad timing or a funding freeze
A company built for easy money cannot raise its next round when investors turn cautious
Many startups funded in the 2021 boom struggled to raise again during the funding slowdown of 2022 and 2023
"How many months of runway does this round buy, and what happens if the next round takes twice as long?"
Governance failure or fraud
Reported numbers do not match reality, or money is used for purposes investors never approved
GoMechanic (2023): investors including Sequoia and Tiger Global said the founders had inflated revenue; the company cut about 70% of jobs and was later sold
"Are the accounts audited, and can I see bank statements and GST filings, not just a dashboard?"

children.text: BluSmart ran an electric cab service, and its co-founders Anmol Singh Jaggi and Puneet Singh Jaggi were also promoters of Gensol Engineering, a company listed on NSE and BSE. In an interim order dated 15 April 2025, SEBI alleged that loans of about ₹262 crore taken to buy around 6,400 electric vehicles had been partly diverted, including towards a ₹43 crore apartment at DLF's The Camellias in Gurugram and transfers to relatives. SEBI barred both brothers from the securities market until further notice and ordered a forensic audit. BluSmart halted ride bookings soon after, leaving drivers and riders stranded.

The lesson for angels: governance risk is not limited to tiny unknown startups. It can sit inside well-funded, high-profile companies, and the only real defence is insisting on verifiable information and independent oversight. These were allegations in an interim regulatory order at the time of SEBI's action.

body.text: Famous investors are not a substitute for your own checks. GoMechanic had Sequoia and Tiger Global. Dunzo had Google and Reliance. Koo had Accel and Tiger Global. A logo on the cap table tells you someone else was convinced, not that the numbers are true or the business will survive.

body.label: MCA: Company and LLP Master Data
body.description: Check a private company's registration status, directors and charges on the Ministry of Corporate Affairs portal, and cross-check filings against what the founder tells you.

children.text: What Failure Means for Your Money

markDefs.definition: Formally recognising that an investment is worth nothing and removing its value from your portfolio records.

children.text: When a startup shuts down, whatever is left goes to creditors first: employees' dues, lenders, vendors and tax authorities. Shareholders come last, and among shareholders, preference holders come before equity holders. In most startup shutdowns, there is little or nothing left by the time anyone reaches the shareholders. Dunzo could not even pay its staff. For planning purposes, a failed angel investment is a
write-off

body.label: Base case for any single seed-stage cheque
body.context: Size every cheque so that losing all of it would not change your life or your financial plans.

children.text: Now picture Farah, who puts ₹5 lakh into each of 20 startups over four years, ₹1 crore in total. Eight years later, her results look like this:

cells: Shut down, total loss
Sold cheaply, partial loss (0.3x)
₹1.5 lakh
₹7.5 lakh
Modest exits (2x)
₹10 lakh
₹30 lakh
One strong winner (20x)

Total
₹1.375 crore

body.title: Farah's 20 startups by outcome (number of companies)

body.caption: A multiple above 1x means the portfolio made money overall; below 1x means it lost money.

body.title: Farah's multiple
body.prompt: Using the table, what is Farah's portfolio multiple? Give your answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Total returned = ₹0 + ₹7.5 lakh + ₹30 lakh + ₹100 lakh = ₹137.5 lakh. Divided by ₹100 lakh invested, that is 1.375x, about 1.38x. Spread over eight years, that works out to roughly 4% a year, below a bank FD, even though one company returned 20x. Sixteen of 20 startups lost money, and a single 20x winner was not big enough to compensate. The next lesson shows why angels need even bigger winners.

children.text: Turning Failure Rates Into Personal Rules
Size for zero.
Decide each cheque by asking what you can afford to lose completely, not by how excited you are.
Build a portfolio, not a bet.
Experienced angels commonly aim for 15 to 25 or more companies over several years, because no one can reliably pick winners in advance.
Diligence the four causes.
Ask the demand, unit economics, runway and governance questions from the table above before every investment.
Do not chase losses.
Putting more money into a struggling company's bridge round to "save" your first cheque is one of the most common ways angels turn one loss into two.

body.title: Warning signs vs signs of resilience

columns.label: Warning signs
points: Growth that stops the moment discounts or cashback stop
Losses per order that grow as the company scales
Less than 6 months of runway with no committed next round
Founder updates that become vague, late or stop entirely

columns.label: Signs of resilience
points: Customers who return and pay without heavy incentives
Unit economics that improve as volume grows
A clear plan to survive if the next round is delayed
Regular, specific updates with audited or verifiable numbers

body.title: Expose the unit economics
body.question: A quick-delivery startup in Pune shows you 40% month-on-month order growth. Which question best tests whether its unit economics are sustainable?
options: How many app downloads did you get last month?
Which famous investors are in your last round?
After delivery cost, discounts and payment fees, how much does the average order make or lose?
How many cities do you plan to launch in next year?
body.explanation: Growth, downloads, investor logos and expansion plans can all look impressive while every order loses money. Profit or loss per order after variable costs is the direct test of unit economics, and it was the central problem for many quick-commerce players.

body.title: Vikram's bridge round
body.scenario: Vikram, an angel in Gurugram, invested ₹20 lakh in a grocery delivery startup 18 months ago. The founder now asks him for ₹10 lakh more in a bridge round. The company has 3 months of runway left. Orders are growing, but losses per order have increased over the last two quarters. The founder says a Series A term sheet is "almost done" but cannot share it.
body.prompt: Should Vikram put in the extra ₹10 lakh? What should he consider?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Treat the new ₹10 lakh as a fresh investment decision. The original ₹20 lakh is a sunk cost; adding money to "protect" it is not a reason on its own.
2. The red flags stack up: very short runway, worsening unit economics and an unverifiable claim about a Series A.
3. Rising losses per order mean growth is making the problem bigger, not smaller. Vikram should ask for per-order economics, a cost-cutting plan and what changes if the Series A never arrives.
4. He should ask to see the term sheet or at least speak to the lead investor. If neither is possible, he should assume there is no committed round.
5. A reasonable decision is to decline, or invest only a small amount he is fully prepared to lose, and only if he gets verifiable information. Many angels turn one loss into two by funding bridges they would never back as new deals.

body.title: Cause or symptom?
body.textWithBlank: Running out of capital is usually the final ___ of a startup's failure, not its root cause.
body.explanation: Money runs out because of deeper problems such as weak demand, broken unit economics, bad timing or governance failures. Those root causes are what diligence should uncover.

cards.definition: When customers keep using and paying for a product without heavy discounts or persuasion.
The profit or loss on a single order or customer after all variable costs.
How much cash a startup spends each month beyond what it earns.
A period when investors sharply cut back, making it hard for startups to raise their next round.
When founders or managers misreport numbers or misuse money, and oversight fails to catch it.
Recognising that an investment is worth nothing.
Money already spent that cannot be recovered and should not drive the next decision.

points: Running out of capital is cited in 70% of startup failures, but it is the symptom; poor product-market fit, bad timing and broken unit economics are common root causes.
Well-funded Indian startups with top investors, including Dunzo, Koo and GoMechanic, still failed, so investor logos are no substitute for your own checks.
In a shutdown, creditors are paid before shareholders, so treat any failed angel investment as a 100% loss.
A portfolio with many losses and one 20x winner can still underperform an FD; angels need rare, very large winners.
Size every cheque for zero, spread money across many companies, and diligence demand, unit economics, runway and governance.
Treat bridge-round requests as new decisions, and never add money just to rescue a sunk cost.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. References to real companies are based on public reports and regulatory orders; some matters involve allegations that may be contested or still under investigation. Farah, Vikram and the portfolio figures are illustrative. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
